  (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), when the legislative body of a local agency limits
 time for public comment, the legislative body of a local agency shall provide at least twice
 the allotted time to a member of the public who utilizes a translator to ensure that non-
 English speakers receive the same opportunity to directly address the legislative body of
 a local agency.”

 In furtherance of Section 54954.3 of the Brown Act, the public is allotted to speak a total

 subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council. As specified in the Brown Act, a speaker
 utilizing a translator will receive twice the amount of time specified.

SUBJECT:  ADOPT RESOLUTION NO. CC 2024-086, A RESOLUTION OF THE
  CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF PALMDALE ADOPTING THE
  JOINT RESOLUTION OF THE BOARD OF SUPERVISORS OF THE
  COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES ACTING ON BEHALF OF THE LOS
  ANGELES COUNTY GENERAL FUND, LOS ANGELES COUNTY
  CONSOLIDATED FIRE PROTECTION DISTRICT, LOS ANGELES
  COUNTY WATERWORKS #40 – ANTELOPE VALLEY, LOS
  ANGELES COUNTY WATERWORKS #40 ACO FUND, THE BOARD
  OF DIRECTORS OF THE COUNTY SANITATION DISTRICT NO. 14
  OF LOS ANGELES COUNTY, AND THE GOVERNING BODIES OF
  THE ANTELOPE VALLEY CEMETERY DISTRICT, ANTELOPE
  VALLEY MOSQUITO AND VECTOR CONTROL DISTRICT,
  ANTELOPE VALLEY RESOURCE CONSERVATION DISTRICT, CITY
  OF PALMDALE, THE ANTELOPE VALLEY – EAST KERN WATER
  AGENCY, AND THE QUARTZ HILL WATER DISTRICT APPROVING
  AND ACCEPTING NEGOTIATED EXCHANGE OF PROPERTY TAX
  REVENUES RESULTING FROM ANNEXATION TO COUNTY
  SANITATION DISTRICT NO. 14

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2024-086, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
  Palmdale adopting the Joint Resolution of the Board of Supervisors of the County
  of Los Angeles acting on behalf of the Los Angeles County General Fund, Los
  Angeles County Consolidated Fire Protection District, Los Angeles County
  Waterworks #40 – Antelope Valley, Los Angeles County Waterworks #40 ACO
  Fund, the Board of Directors of the County Sanitation District No. 14 of Los
  Angeles County, and the governing bodies of the Antelope Valley Cemetery
  District, Antelope Valley Mosquito and Vector Control District, Antelope Valley
  Resource Conservation District, City of Palmdale, the Antelope Valley – East Kern
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Resolution No. CC 2024-086
November 20, 2024
Page 2

  Water Agency, and the Quartz Hill Water District approving and accepting
  negotiated exchange of property tax revenues resulting from annexation to
  County Sanitation District No. 14;

  2. Authorize the Mayor to execute the Joint Resolution No. CC 2024-086, approving
  and accepting the negotiated exchange of property tax revenues resulting from
  the annexation of territory to County Sanitation District No. 14 in the annexation
  entitled Annexation No. 456; and,

  3. Authorize the Mayor to execute the Los Angeles County Joint Resolution,
  approving and accepting the negotiated exchange of property tax revenues
  resulting from the annexation of territory to County Sanitation District No. 14 in the
  annexation entitled Annexation No. 456.

BACKGROUND

The County Sanitation District No. 14 of Los Angeles County has requested that the City
enter into a tax sharing agreement for parcel number 3204-024-055, parcels 3204-089-
001 through 028 and parcels 3204-090-001 through 025, as shown in the attached
Annexation No. 456 Map. These parcels are part of a proposed single-family residential
housing development (Tract No. 60431-01) located between 70th and 75th Streets West,
south of Avenue M. The project’s developer, Lancaster Villas LLC, has requested
annexation into County Sanitation District No. 14. This annexation is a condition of the
development’s entitlement and is required before receiving sewer service.

In accordance with the Revenue and Tax Code (Sections 99 and 99.01), any time there
is a jurisdictional change that results in a special district providing a new service not
previously provided to an area, the law requires the governing bodies of all local
agencies that receive a portion of that property tax determine by resolution the amount
of the annual tax increase to be transferred to that special district. The existing ad
velorem tax revenue based on the property’s assessed value received by agencies will
not change. This action only affects that portion of future tax revenues based on
increases in assessed property value.

DISCUSSION

Adopting this Joint Resolution will approve the City’s tax-sharing agreement between
public agencies currently receiving tax revenue from these parcels and County
Sanitation District No. 14, which through the referenced annexation, will provide services
to this parcel for the first time. All the referenced agencies and special districts will
execute and are party to the same Joint Resolution.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Resolution No. CC 2024-086
November 20, 2024
Page 3

FISCAL IMPACT

The current property tax share ratio for the City of Palmdale within the area of this
annexation is 6.6294%. This Council action will allocate 0.0396% of any future tax
increase to County Sanitation District No. 14. This results in a net City tax share rate of
6.5897%. For example, a tax increase based on the assessed property value for these
parcels will generate an additional $100 in total property tax. The City would receive an
additional $6.5897 of this increase and the County Sanitation District No. 14 would
receive $0.0396. This allocation follows the State Revenue and Taxation Code, and the
allocation formula is established and calculated by the Los Angeles County Auditor-
Controller.

STRATEGIC PLAN

Goal II: Ensure the long-term fiscal health of the City and maintain funding for
  services.

  A. Manage resources, costs, and liabilities to ensure the City’s long-term fiscal
  health.

SUBJECT:  APPROVE AGREEMENT WITH SVA ARCHITECT, INC. FOR DESIGN
  AND CONSTRUCTION ADMINISTRATION SERVICES FOR PN 878,
  CHIMBOLE CULTURAL CENTER- CITY LIBRARY-FINANCE
  RENOVATION PROJECT, FOR A TOTAL NOT TO EXCEED AMOUNT
  OF $ 1,915,070 FOR A TOTAL TERM OF 540 WORKING DAYS FROM
  THE DATE OF THE NOTICE TO PROCEED

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Approve Agreement No. A-9097 with SVA Architect, Inc. for the design and
  construction administration services for PN 878, Chimbole Cultural Center-Library-
  Finance Renovation Project, for a total not to exceed amount of $1,915,070, which
  includes a contract amount of $1,665,070 plus a 15% contingency amount of
  $250,000; for a total term of 540 working days from the date of the notice to
  proceed; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager and her designee to execute Agreement No. A-9097
  with SVA Architect, Inc. including minimal and/or non-substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

The City seeks a consultant to perform architectural and engineering design services for
three (3) existing buildings: the Chimbole Cultural Center (Cultural Center), Palmdale City
Library, and the Finance/Operations Department; Project No. 878, Chimbole-Library-
Finance Renovation Project.

The Cultural Center is a two-story, 22,000-square-foot facility that requires remodeling
and renovation to repair the damage caused by fire and water from an incident in
December 2022. In addition to the tenant improvements, this project will provide upgrades
and improvements to the exterior of the building, including accessibility, lighting, and
parking upgrades.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Award of PN 878, Agreement No. A-9097
November 20, 2024
Page 2

The existing City Library, with 13,000 square feet, will expand to the south, eliminating
the breezeway, connect to the Cultural Center, and utilize some of the first floor of the
Cultural Center for Library functions. The approximate Library expansion is 4,000 square
feet. The existing Library will be renovated to provide more up-to-date technology for
patron’s use, including internet access, computer stations, and check-out laptops.

The existing Finance/Operation Department, with 6,500 square feet of office space,
requires a space study to efficiently maximize the area for the proposed use. The study
will include assessments and recommendations for improvements to the existing
restrooms, elevators’ compliance with ADA and the existing HVAC systems, and
electrical, plumbing, and roofing conditions. The consultant will identify the occupancy
impacts on the existing site entitlements and will provide the study for staff review prior to
any tenant improvements being designed.

Due to the fire damage at the Cultural Center, staff anticipates unforeseen structural
conditions that may arise and will be added to the design scope. Therefore, the staff is
recommending a 15% design contingency.

DISCUSSION

The project was advertised electronically through PlanetBids on June 10, 2024. Over 269
vendors were notified. Twenty-seven vendors downloaded the bid documents for review,
and twelve vendors registered as designers/architects.

On June 18, 2024, thirteen designers/architects attended the mandatory pre-bid meeting.
On July 9, 2024, twelve proposals were received and evaluated including one local
vendor. Upon review, the following five designers were interviewed:

Bidder  Location  Amount
1. SVA Architect, Inc.  Santa Ana, CA  $ 1,599,963
2. TSK Architects  Los Angeles, CA  $ 1,794,196
3. Moore Ruble Yudell  Santa Monica, CA  $ 1,785,000
4. SGH Architects  Redlands, CA  $ 1,883,000
5. Perkins Eastman  Costa Mesa, CA  $ 2,160,000

Two designers were selected for negotiations: SVA Architect, Inc. and Perkins Eastman.
SVA Architect, Inc. revised their design scope to include Furniture, Fixtures, & Equipment
(FF&E), low voltage fire alarm system, security cameras and monitors, audiovisual
packages including videoconferencing, presentations, and Wi-Fi networking throughout
for the Cultural Center and Library. Perkins Eastman was not able to offer a revised
proposal.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Award of PN 878, Agreement No. A-9097
November 20, 2024
Page 3

Additional consulting services (if required) would include Topographic Survey,
Underground Utility Survey, and Reimbursable allowance:

Bidder  Location  Amount
1. SVA Architect, Inc. (Revised proposal)  Santa Ana, Ca  $ 1,598,070.00
  Additional consulting services  $ 67,000.00
2. Perkins Eastman  Costa Mesa, CA  $ 2,070,000
  Additional consulting services  $ 90,000

The SVA Architects, Inc. presentation and project approach are more detailed and
comprehensive compared to Perkins Eastman.

Staff recommends the award of the design and construction administration services to
SVA Architects, Inc.

$1,915,070; Funds are budgeted and available in FY 2024-25 in Account Nos.

follows:

   City Council Staff Report
DATE:  NOVEMBER 20, 2024

TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL

FROM:  PUBLIC WORKS DEPARTMENT
  CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT PROGRAM DIVISION

DISTRICT:  ALL

SUBJECT:  APPROVE AGREEMENT WITH BOWMAN CONSULTING GROUP
  FOR DESIGN SERVICES FOR PN 895, HIGHWAY SAFETY
  IMPROVEMENT  PROGRAM  AND  TRAFFIC  SIGNAL
  IMPROVEMENTS PROJECT, FOR A TOTAL NOT TO EXCEED
  AMOUNT OF $438,863 FOR A TERM OF 215 WORKING DAYS FROM
  THE DATE OF THE NOTICE TO PROCEED

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Approve Agreement No. A-9107 with Bowman Consulting Group for design
  services for PN 895, Highway Safety Improvement Program (HSIP) and Traffic
  Signal Improvements Project for preliminary engineering/design for $438,863
  which includes a contract amount of $389,876 plus a 10% contingency amount of
  $38,987 and administration amount of $10,000 for a term of 215 working days from
  the date of the notice to proceed; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to execute the Agreement No. A-
  9107 with Bowman Consulting Group, including minimal and/or non-substantial
  changes.

BACKGROUND

In September 2022, Caltrans awarded the City Highway Safety Improvement Program
(HSIP) grant funds for City-wide traffic signal modernization and pedestrian
replacement. Caltrans HSIP authorized this project in April 2024 for the preliminary
engineering/design phase at $450,000 with a $50,000 match for local return. The
preliminary engineering/design phase will find and identify deficiencies at selected traffic
signalized intersections and complete a final Plans, Specifications, and Estimates
(PS&E). The PS&E will itemize those deficiencies that include, but are not limited to,
replacing old wire, replace street signs with new reflectorized signs, installation of new
 Report to Mayor and City Council

LED signal heads with backplates equipped with yellow reflective borders, ADA
improvements such as more lead time for pedestrian intervals, high visibility pedestrian
crosswalks, ADA curb ramps, and pedestrian push buttons that include
Audible/Accessible Pedestrian Signal and/or touchless. These ADA improvements meet
all general standards for ADA requirements. To anticipate unforeseen traffic signal
conditions, we recommend adding a 10% design contingency to the design scope.

DISCUSSION

On July 25, 2024, a Request for Proposal (RFP) was advertised electronically through
Planet Bids that included both local and non-local companies for engineering design
with a sealed bid process. The sealed bids were submitted separately from the
proposals. Only the top-ranking bid will have their sealed bid opened. On August 22,
2024, four bids were received. After reviewing the proposals, two bids were rejected and
two bids moved on to the interview portion. After the interviews, Bowman Consulting
Group was the top-ranking bid, and their sealed bid was opened. See below:

Bidder  Location  Amount
1. Bowman Consulting Group  Brea, CA  $389,876

  RECITALS

  WHEREAS, City desires to engage PROJECT DESIGNER to perform certain
technical and professional services, as provided herein, in connection with that
certain project identified as PN 895, HSIP Cycle 11 Traffic Signal Improvement.

  WHEREAS, PROJECT DESIGNER represents that PROJECT DESIGNER

1  DESCRIPTION OF WORK

1.1  The City hereby engages PROJECT DESIGNER, and PROJECT DESIGNER
accepts such engagement, to perform the following design professional services in a
manner satisfactory to CITY:

For PN 895, HSIP Cycle 11 Traffic Signal Improvements. Complete a full and
thorough field investigation to collect data and measurements at each of the twenty-
five (25) intersection locations, including, but not limited to. The purpose of the City’s
request is to modify selected traffic signals by finding deficiencies and replacing old
traffic signal infrastructure. The work may include, but not limited to replacing old
wire, new street name signs, new LED signal heads that have backplates equipped
with retroreflective borders at all city traffic signals, which are more visible and
conspicuous in both daytime and nighttime conditions, additional upgrading the traffic
signals to meet ADA standards, including but not limited to leading pedestrian
intervals, pedestrian high visibility crosswalks, curb ramps, pedestrian push buttons
that include Audible/Accessible Pedestrian Signal (APS) and/or touchless. All
necessary items for California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and the National
Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). All necessary items for Caltrans. The use of Virtual
Project Management (VPM) for project support and planning. All necessary items for
Southern California Edison to identify any complications, which includes load
calculations and/or load diagrams can be required when planning for traffic signals.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Approve Requisition No. 250493 with SiteOne Landscape Supply, LLC for
  landscape aggregate, boulders, and materials in an amount not to exceed
  $252,945 for Fiscal Year 2024-25; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to execute Requisition No. 250493
  and the resulting Purchase Order with SiteOne Landscape Supply, LLC for an
  amount not to exceed $252,945, including minimal and/or non-substantial
  changes.

BACKGROUND

The Maintenance Division uses landscape rock aggregate, boulders, and materials for
landscape renovation and maintenance projects at City parks and facility grounds,
Palmdale Transportation Center, Park and Rides, General Benefit Landscape areas, and
Landscape Maintenance Districts.

The City released an Invitation for Bid (IFB) No. 22-007-3400 for Landscape Aggregate,
Boulders, and Materials in October 2022. SiteOne Landscape Supply, LLC was the
lowest responsive bidder and issued an intent to award in January 2023, for Fiscal Year
2022-23, with an option to extend the purchase order contract two additional fiscal years.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Approve Requisition No. 250493 with SiteOne Landscape Supply, LLC
November 20, 2024
Page 2

In October 2023, the first option to extend the purchase order contract was exercised
for an additional one-year period for Fiscal Year 2023-24 which included completion of
the first phase of the North Pelona Vista Park trail renovations.

DISCUSSION

With this requisition, the second and final option to extend the purchase order contract
will be exercised for an additional one-year period through June 30, 2025 (Fiscal Year
2024-25) in the amount of $252,945.

Landscape enhancement projects, and the materials purchased from SiteOne Landscape
Supply, LLC, are essential for beautifying and sustaining city grounds and community
green spaces, maintaining landscape quality, and providing safe and attractive public
spaces and infrastructure.

Projects identified for Fiscal Year 2024-25 include the following locations:

    Palmdale Transportation Center round-about and planters
    Pelona Vista Park trail maintenance and Park & Ride frontage planter
    Desert Sands Park frontage planter
    Palmdale Blvd Frontage Rd between 3rd Street East and 2nd Street East
    Palmdale Blvd center medians east and west of 3rd Street East
    LMD 41 planters (located near Rancho Vista Blvd and Avenue P-8 between 20th
  Street West and 22nd Street West)
    LMD 122 planters (located near Pearblossom Hwy and Avenue S-11 between 37th
  Street East and 40th Street East)
    LMD 51 planters (located near Avenue R between Amethyst St and 50th Street
  East)

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2024-084, a Resolution of the City Council of the City
  of Palmdale to adopt the City of Palmdale Local Road Safety Plan; and,

  2. Authorize the Mayor to execute Resolution No. CC 2024-084, a Resolution of the
  City Council of the City of Palmdale to adopt the City of Palmdale Local Road
  and Safety plan.

BACKGROUND

The Palmdale Local Road Safety Plan (LRSP) serves as the City’s guide for
transportation improvements in Palmdale, with the core goals of improving safety for all
road users. The LRSP:

    Aligns with the vision and goals in the Palmdale 2045 General Plan and the
  Palmdale Sustainable Transportation Plan.
    Is an addendum to the Sustainable Transportation Plan adopted on June 7, 2023.
    Develops safety measures using the four E’s of safety: Engineering, Enforcement,
  Education, and Emergency Response to encourage safer driver behavior and
  lower severity outcomes.
    Examined crash data and identified locations that will benefit from safety
  enhancements.
    Includes recommendations to improve safety at specific high-crash locations and
  reduce serious injury and fatal collisions.

Through the LRSP the City continues its safety efforts by identifying areas of emphasis
and systemic recommendations to enhance safety for all road users. The consulting firm
Kimley-Horn worked with City staff to develop the LRSP.

DISCUSSION

The LRSP is a prerequisite for obtaining certain grant funds made available under various
federal, state, regional, and local programs. The Council’s adoption of the LRSP will help
strengthen the City’s standing when applying for future transportation grants with a focus
on enhancing transportation safety in Palmdale. For example, a Council-adopted LRSP
is required when applying through the US Department of Transportation’s (USDOT)
Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) for funding toward improvements to surface
roadways, including pedestrian and bicycle infrastructure.

 Executive Summary

The City of Palmdale adopted a Sustainable Transportation Plan on June 7, 2023, and the Local
Roadway Safety Plan (LRSP) is an addendum to that plan. The LRSP identifies additional
emphasis areas to inform and guide further safety evaluation of the City’s transportation network.
The plan analyzes crash data previously used in the Sustainable Transportation Plan. With
discussion from City Staff, and the public, new specific locations were identified. The Local
Roadway Safety Plan is built off the analysis of the Safety Plan section of the Sustainable
Transportation Plan. Although the methodology is similar, new analysis was conducted based on
additional project locations, and emphasis areas. The Local Roadway Safety Plan is an
addendum that shows the Citys’ of Palmdale dedication to implement effective roadway safety
strategies, such as traffic calming measures, improved signage and markings, pedestrian and
cyclist-friendly infrastructure, and enhance driver education, and awareness programs. By
actively addressing safety concerns and collaborating with local authorities and stakeholders, the
City of Palmdale aims to create a safer and more efficient transportation network. Through the
systemic analysis for both the Sustainable Transportation Plan and the Local Roadway Safety
Plan it continues to align with the opportunity for the City to:

  1. Identify factors in the transportation network that reduce safety for all roadway users;
  2. Improve safety at specific high-crash locations, and reduce serious injury and fatal
  collisions, and
  3. Develop safety measures using the four E’s of safety: Engineering, Enforcement,
  Education, and Emergency Response to encourage safer driver behavior and lower
  severity outcomes. With this plan, the City continues its safety efforts by identifying areas
  of emphasis and systemic recommendations to enhance safety.
The City’s vision is to enhance the transportation network and reduce traffic fatalities and serious
injury related crashes, and the goals for the City of Palmdale are in support of General Plan Goal
CM-1:

  •  Build and maintain a transportation system that is safe and comfortable for travelers of all
  modes regardless of age or ability.

As well as its sub-goals:

  •  CM-1.1 Roadway design. Design and maintain the public right-of-way through a
  complete streets approach that facilitates safe, comfortable, and efficient travel for all
  roadway users.
  •  CM-1.2 Modal conflicts. Use a systemic safety approach to proactively identify
  opportunities to improve safety where conflicts between users exist.

  3
   •  CM-1.3 Network gaps. Identify and program mitigation measures for gaps and
  deficiencies in the transportation system to accommodate each major transportation
  mode.
  •  CM-1.4 Speed management. Include speed reducing elements along local and
  connector roadways and within all new private development projects.

The General Plan Goal CM-1 are furthered by this plan through these targeted objectives:

  Objective #1: Identify high-risk crash zones.

  Objective #2: Demonstrate the significance of a comprehensive safety program and the
  systematic approach.

  Objective #3: Develop safety improvement plans for near-,mid-, and long-term.

  Objective #4:Idenitfy safety projects for consideration of funding through HSIP and other
  program sources.

This plan analyzes a range of crash data (January 1, 2017 – December 31, 2021) and roadway
characteristics to assess historic trends, and areas of increasing concern. While the COVID-19
pandemic altered traffic conditions and crash patterns in 2020 and 2021, these years were
ultimately included to understand recent trends.

Furthermore, an analysis of collision history was conducted to identify locations that exhibit a
higher risk of collisions, based on either their past collision history or their similarities to other
locations with frequent collision pattern. Through a comprehensive network screening process,
specific locations within the City were pinpointed as having the greatest impact with
implementation of safety enhancements. Additionally, collision risk factors for the entire network
were derived. These findings informed the identification and prioritization of engineering and non-
infrastructure safety measures aimed at addressing specific roadway characteristics and
behaviors that contribute to motor vehicle collisions involving active transportation users.

Emphasis areas were developed by revisiting the vision and goals developed at the beginning of
the planning process and comparing them with the trends and patterns identified in the collision
analysis.

  Emphasis Area #1: Unsignalized Intersection Improvements

  Emphasis Area #2: Vulnerable Road Users Improvements (Pedestrians & Bicyclists)

  Emphasis Area #3: Traffic Calming Improvement

The following 10 project locations were chosen as three (3) systemic projects and seven (7)
corridor projects:

  1. 30th Street East and Olive Drive
  2. 30th Street East and Avenue Q

  4
  3. 20th St East : Avenue Q to Palmdale Boulevard
 4. Avenue R-4 and 25th Street East
 5. Avenue Q-7: 2nd Street East to Stanridge Avenue
 6. 2nd Street East: Avenue Q-7 to Avenue Q-4
 7. 3rd Street East: Palmdale Boulevard to Avenue Q-7
 8. Division Street and Kimberly Lane
 9. Avenue R-4 and Palm Vista Avenue
 10. Cisero Drive and 57th Street East

These locations were identified through a comprehensive analysis process that considered
various factors such as collision histories, stakeholder engagement, observed collision patterns,
and differing characteristics. The goal was to gain valuable insights into potential systemic safety
countermeasures that the City can implement to achieve cost-effective safety benefits. It is
important to note that these locations were not necessarily chosen based solely on the number
of collisions, but rather on their diverse characteristics, providing a wide range of solutions
applicable to most areas within the City. The findings from these project locations should not be
seen as a prioritized project list, but rather as opportunities for systemic and corridor safety
enhancements throughout the City.

Near-term action items were identified to accelerate the City’s achievement of the goals and vision
of this LRSP. The City may:

  •  Actively seek other funding opportunities to improve safety for all modal users,
  •  Collaborate with established safety partners & neighboring municipalities as
  improvements are made to create a cohesive transportation network, and
  •  Iteratively evaluate existing and proposed transportation safety programs and capital
  improvements to design a safer transportation network in the City of Palmdale

These recommendations provide the City of Palmdale with a look-ahead for safety improvements
that can be applied systemically. Additionally, this information can be used to help the City apply
for grants and other funding opportunities to implement these safety improvements.

To develop these countermeasures, references were made to both the California Local Roadway
Safety manual (LRSM) and Caltrans Proven Safety Countermeasures, while adhering to the
principles of the Safe System Approach. The potential benefit and cost of each countermeasure
were evaluated. By extrapolating the potential benefits of these countermeasures to locations with
similar design characteristics, proactive safety enhancements can be implemented, regardless of
past collision history, to prevent future safety challenges. Additionally, this information can be
utilized to support the City’s application for grants and other funding opportunities to implement
safety improvements. Regular monitoring and updates will be conducted based on the analysis
performed in this plan. A comprehensive plan update will be required five years after the City
Council adopts this plan, which will maintain eligibility for HSIP funding.

 Introduction

The Local Roadway Safety Plan identifies emphasis areas that will inform and guide further
evaluation of the City’s transportation network. These areas include the type of crashes, specific
locations, and notable relationships between current efforts and crash history. The plan analyzes
crash data both in aggregate and at specific locations to identify areas with high crash rates, high-
risk locations, and city-wide trends and patterns. This analysis of crash history throughout the
City’s transportation network presents several opportunities:

  1. Identify factors in the transportation network that reduce safety for all roadway users;
  2. Improve safety at specific high-crash locations; and,
  3. Develop safety measures using the four E’s of safety (Engineering, Enforcement,
  Education, and Emergency Response) to encourage safer driver behavior and lower
  severity outcomes.

Palmdale has taken steps to enhance all modal safety throughout the City and with this plan,
Palmdale is continuing to prioritize safety in its planning processes. The Local Roadway Safety
Plan serves as an addendum to the Sustainable Transportation Plan. It complements the broader
goals and visions outlined in the Sustainable Transportation Plan by specifically addressing the
safety aspect of the City’s transportation network. By identifying emphasis areas and analyzing
crash data, the Local Roadway Safety Plan helps inform and guide further safety evaluation and
improvement efforts. This integration ensures that safety considerations are integrated into the
overall planning and development of the City’s transportation system, promoting a holistic and
sustainable approach to transportation. The following are the general six step process that was
used as a framework when developing the Local Roadway Safety Plan (LRSP):

Step 1: Establish Leadership

  Identify a Champion who will lead the LRSP development process.

  Convene a Working Group to collaborate on the development of the plan.

Step 2: Analyze Safety Data

  Gather relevant safety data, including crash data and other safety data sources.

  Conduct data analysis to identify trends and patterns.

Step 3: Determine Emphasis Areas

  Identify specific areas of focus for the LRSP based on the analysis of safety data.

  Set objectives and performance measures for each emphasis area.

Step 4: Identify Strategies

  6
   Categorize and review potential strategies that can address the identified emphasis
  areas.

  Propose ordinances and policies as necessary to support the strategies.

Step 5: Prioritize and Incorporate Strategies

  Determine priorities among the identified strategies based on the objectives and
  performance measures.

  Determine the intended implementation approach for each strategy.

  Incorporate the strategies into the LRSP.

Step 6: Evaluate and Update the LRSP

  Monitor the progress of implementing the strategies outlined in the LRSP.

  Conduct periodic evaluations to assess the effectiveness of the plan.

  Maintain the LRSP as a living document that can be updated and revised as needed.

The intent of the LRSP is to increase road safety awareness, reduce fatal and severe-injury
crashes, develop partnerships, support grant applications, and prioritize investment in traffic
safety.

 3. Process

The LRSP and the Sustainable Transportation Plan share a similar process and methodology in
identifying safety issues, involving stakeholders, and utilizing data to inform decision-making. In
the development of the LRSP, the analysis includes a combination of quantitative and qualitative
measures to identify locations with high crash frequency or crash rates. This analysis also
considers crash type and severity patterns to determine the causes of crashes and potential
effective countermeasures. Both the LRSP and STP analyzed intersections and roadways
utilizing four collision metrics for analysis:

  •  Number of Collisions- involves counting the total number of reported crashes that occurred
  at a specific intersection or roadway. It provides an overview of the frequency of collisions
  in that area.
  •  Critical Crash Rate (HSM Ch. 4)- quantifies the rate at which severe or fatal crashes occur
  within a given area or a specific roadway segment. A higher critical crash rate indicates a
  higher risk of severe accidents.
  •  Probability of Specific Crash Types Exceeding Threshold Proportion (HSM Ch. 4)-
  assesses the likelihood of specific types of crashes exceeding a predetermined threshold
  proportion. It helps identify crash types that occur more frequently than expected and
  require targeted interventions.
  •  Equivalent Property Damage Only (HSM Ch. 4)-estimates the total cost of crashes in
  terms of property damage. It allows for a comparison of crash severity and economic
  impacts across different intersections or roadways.

  The LRSP establishes a systematic framework for identifying and analyzing safety concerns
  and proposing safety improvements. The LRSP utilizes updated data and incorporates
  additional analysis compared to the STP. This includes examining pedestrian and bicyclist
  collisions within a 250-foot radius near schools, conducting network screening using the
  Equivalent Property Damage Only Method, and analyzing traffic calming measures for areas
  with aggressive driving/traffic concerns.

  In terms of countermeasure selection, both plans utilize evidence-based approaches. The
  LRSP incorporates Crash modification Factors (CMFs), which quantify the expected rate of
  crash reduction from specific countermeasures. By analyzing these collision metrics, the
  LRSP and STP can effectively assess the safety performance of the City’s roadway network
  and identify areas where targeted interventions may be necessary to improve safety and
  reduce the occurrence of severe crashes. More information about the analysis techniques and
  guidance of the LRSP can be found in the Safety Section in Palmdale’s Sustainable
  Transportation Plan in Section 3.

9. Countermeasure Toolbox

This section provides information on general identified issues, crash reduction factors,
improvements, and countermeasures identified for the City of Palmdale, as well as for specific
project locations identified as part of this analysis. Countermeasures for each of the Safety Project
Conceptual Plans are based on data analysis, stakeholder input, and site visits.

9.1 Infrastructure Improvements
9.1.1 Countermeasure Selection Process
Part D of the HSM provides information on Crash Modification Factors(CMFs) for roadway
segments, intersections, interchanges, special facilities, and road networks. CMFs are used to
estimate the safety effects of highway improvements, specifically to compare and select highway
safety improvements. A CMF less than 1.0 indicates that a treatment has the potential to reduce
crashes. A CMF greater than 1.0 indicates that a treatment has the potential to increase crashes.
A Crash Reduction Factor (CRF) is directly connected to the CMF and is “mathematically defined
as (1 – CMF) (the higher the CRF, the greater the expected reduction in crashes) 1.” CMFs can
help decision makers weigh potential alternative projects but are only one measure of a project's
value and should be considered part of a larger decision-making process. Furthermore, it is
important to note that not all CMFs are as reliable as others. The FHWA maintains a federal
depository of CMFs and includes a star rating system to help users determine which CMFs are
bolstered by the best and most thorough research. Key factors to consider when applying CMFs
include:

  1.  Selection of an appropriate CMF;
  2.  Estimation of crashes without treatment;
  3.  Application of CMFs by type and severity; and,
  4.  Estimation of the combined effect for multiple treatments.

Examples of Safety Countermeasures can be found through several sources. This Report utilizes
the countermeasures found in the California LRSM and the CMF Clearinghouse (CMF CH)
website. The Caltrans Proven Safety Countermeasures guidance also informed the selection of
these countermeasures. Countermeasures for each of the Safety Project Case Studies are based
on the data analysis and site visits. Additional countermeasures were identified for the high-level
issues on a city-wide level and are discussed in Section 9.

 9.2 Citywide Countermeasure Toolbox
This evaluation considered citywide trends to identify countermeasures that would likely provide
the most benefit with widespread implementation. Table 3 outlines the citywide safety project
opportunities, which is also referred to as the “Countermeasure Toolbox”. Within the toolbox, the
description of the countermeasure along with its Local Roadway Safety Manual (LRSM) ID
number is listed. The next column, Crash Reduction Factor (CRF), are “multiplicative factors
used to estimate the expected reduction in number of crashes after implementing a given
countermeasure at a specific site (the higher the CRF, the greater the expected reduction in
crashes).” For each of these countermeasures, a planning level benefit/cost analysis was
completed.

Applying the benefit/cost at the citywide level was estimated assuming some randomness in
crash distribution. The location characteristics, such as whether there is a traffic signal, and the
type of crashes, were used at the citywide level to calculate an average cost of crashes that the
countermeasure might reduce. The benefit per location was then factored out to a 20-year
lifecycle savings, with an Opinion of Project Probable Cost (OPCC) for the initial installation
costs and a per-year maintenance cost estimate. The cost shown in Table 3 should be
considered initial planning costs using 2022 dollars and not assumed final.

In order to prioritize the projects in the countermeasure toolbox, the following section highlights
countermeasures that are appropriate for the networks shown in Section 7. Near-term projects
can be implemented within the next two years, mid-term projects within the next five years, and
long term projects within the next ten years.

 10. Funding Sources & Next Steps

10.1 Funding
Competitive funding resources are available to assist in the development and implementation of
safety projects in Palmdale. Similar to the Safety Plan in the STP the City should continue to seek
available funding and grant opportunities from local, state, and federal resources to accelerate
their ability to implement safety improvements throughout Palmdale. This section provides a high-
level introduction to some of the main funding programs and grants for which the City can apply.

10.1.1 Highway Safety Improvement Program
The Highway Safety Improvement Program (HSIP) is a Federal program that apportions funding
as a lump sum for each state, which is then divided among apportioned programs. These flexible
funds can be used for projects to preserve or improve safety conditions and performance on any
Federal-aid highway, bridge projects on any public road, facilities for non-motorized
transportation, and other project types. Safety improvement projects eligible for this funding
include:

•  New or upgraded traffic signals
•  Upgraded guard rails
•  Pedestrian warning flashing beacons
•  Marked high visibility crosswalks
•  Other projects listed in the Caltrans Local Road Safety Manual

California’s local HSIP focuses on infrastructure projects with national recognized crash reduction
factors. Normally HSIP call-for-projects is made at an interval of one to two years. The applicant
must be a city, a county, or a tribal government federally recognized within the State of California.

Additional information regarding this program at the Federal level can be found online at:
https://safety.fhwa.dot.gov/hsip/. California specific HSIP information – including dates for
upcoming call for projects - can be found at: Local Highway Safety Improvement Program (HSIP)
| Caltrans. The locations and countermeasures discussed in this analysis can be used to develop
a grant application to the next round of Highway Safety Improvement Program funding. The next
round of funding is expected in fall 2024.

10.1.2 Caltrans Active Transportation Program
Caltrans Active Transportation Program (ATP) is a statewide funding program, created in 2013,
consolidating several federal and state programs. The ATP funds projects that encourage
increased mode share for walking and bicycling, improve mobility and safety for non-motorized
users, enhance public health, and decrease greenhouse gas emissions. Projects eligible for this
funding include:

•  Bicycle and pedestrian infrastructure projects
•  Bicycle and pedestrian planning projects (e.g., safe routes to school)
•  Non-infrastructure programs (education and enforcement)

  28
 This program funding is provided annually. The ATP call for projects typically comes out in the
spring. Information on this program and cycles can be found online at: Active Transportation
Program (ATP) | Caltrans.

10.1.3 California SB 1
The California SB (Senate Bill) 1 is a landmark transportation investment to rebuild California by
fixing neighborhood streets, freeways, and bridges in communities across California and targeting
funds toward transit and congested trade and commute corridor improvements.

California’s state-maintained transportation infrastructure will receive roughly half of SB 1
revenue: $26 billion. The other half will go to local roads, transit agencies and an expansion of
the state’s growing network of pedestrian and cycle routes. Each year, this new funding will be
used to tackle deferred maintenance needs both on the state highway system and the local road
system, including:

•  Local Street and Road Maintenance and Rehabilitation: $1.5 billion
  o  This funding is dedicated to improving local road maintenance, rehabilitation, and/or
  safety through projects such as restriping and repaving.
•  Bike and Pedestrian Projects: $100 million
  o  This will go to cities, counties, and regional transportation agencies to build or
  convert more bike paths, crosswalks, and sidewalks. It is a significant increase in
  funding for these projects through the ATP.
•  Local Planning Grants: $25 million
10.1.4 California Office of Traffic Safety Grants
This program has funding for projects related to traffic safety, including transportation safety
education and encouragement activities. Grant applications must be supported by local collision
data (such as the data analyzed in this report) and must relate to the following priority program
areas:

  o  Alcohol Impaired Driving
  o  Distracted Driving
  o  Drug-Impaired Emergency Medical Services
  o  Motorcycle Safety
  o  Occupant Protection
  o  Pedestrian and Bicycle Safety
  o  Police Traffic Services
  o  Public Relations, Advertising, and Marketing Program
  o  Roadway Safety and Traffic Records

  29
 10.1.5 SCAG Sustainable Communities Program
This program is an innovative vehicle for promoting local jurisdictional efforts to test local planning
tools. The Sustainable Communities Program (SCP) provides direct technical assistance to
SCAG member jurisdictions to complete planning and policy efforts to implement the regional
Sustainable Communities Strategies (SCS). Grants are available in the following three categories:

•  Integrated Land Use

  o  Sustainable Land Use Planning
  o  Transit Oriented Development (TOD)
  o  Land Use & Transportation Integration

•  Active Transportation

  o  Bicycle Planning
  o  Pedestrian Planning
  o  Safe Routes to School Plans

•  Green Region

  o  Natural Resource Plans
  o  Climate Action Plans (CAPs)
  o  Green House Gas (GHG) Reduction programs

10.1.6 Safe Streets and Roads for All (SS4A) Grant Program
This program has allocated $1 billion annually for the next four years for local cities, counties,
MPOs, and other roadway owners (excepting state DOTs) for safety improvement grants for
Safety Planning, education, enforcement, and roadway improvements. This program is not
benefit / cost based. Evaluation criteria are oriented to the project’s alignment with the Safe
Systems approach. There is a 20% local match requirement (can be in-kind contribution via staff
billable hours). Planning grants are open to any eligible agency and Implementation grants are
open to agencies with a completed safety plan such as Local Roadway Safety Plan. Planning
grants are expected to range from $100 thousand to $1 million and Implementation grants are
expected to range from $1 million to $20 million. Grant applications are expected to be due in
July 2024.

10.1.6 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act
In November 2021, the President signed into law the $1.2 trillion Infrastructure Investment and
Jobs Act. In addition to the SS4A grant program described above, this law provides billions of
dollars in additional funding for improvements and investment in the transportation sector
nationwide. The law provides $30 billion in funding over five years for competitive RAISE grants
for transportation projects, as well as additional funding for repair and environmental mitigation
projects. As these grant programs continue to be developed, City can position itself by
identifying potential projects and programs to pursue.

 10.2 Implementation Plan
Once the Local Roadway Safety Plan has been completed, the city can plan to regularly review
and monitor crash data for trends and changes. The County can also plan to prioritize and
implement certain improvements that were identified in this plan.

10.2.1 Monitoring
The City can plan to regularly monitor the success of the LRSP and its related implementations
by performing the following steps. This before and after analysis can be performed throughout
the year. The City can also meet with the Sheriffs Department on a regular basis to discuss
roadway safety issues and compare to the latest crash analysis.

•  Pull yearly crash data from Crossroads database to determine year-over year trend
•  Utilize Crossroads or GIS software to review the number of collisions occurring at specific
  locations. Locations where improvements have been made should receive priority for
  monitoring; and,
•  Based upon changes in collision activity, determine efficacy of improvements and adjust
  strategies going forward.

10.2.2 Analysis Update
The city can plan to update the analysis every two years as part of a monitoring program. Every
5 years the city will perform a major update to the analysis and the Local Roadway Safety Plan
by performing the following steps. This update will maintain eligibility for the HSP grant funding
for the city. The analysis should continue to focus on both systemic and location specific safety
needs.

  1. Obtain updated Statewide Integrated Traffic Records System (SWITRS) collision data
  from the City’s collision database;
  2. Use Excel software to update the collision trend analysis completed in Section 7, continue
  to compare new collision to historic trends;
  3. Update the roadway shapefile with any new or upgraded roadways;
  4. Update the intersection shapefile with any new or upgraded intersections;
  5. Re-run the GIS-based safety collision tool to determine the number of collisions at
  intersections and roadways within the updated study period. The City can plan to run the
  collision tool for all collisions, as well as the collision types identified in Section 6
  6. Update the collision analysis performed in this report, including the collision analysis
  tables shown in Section 7 Collision Network Screening Analysis Report; and,
  7. Review the Collision Toolbox to determine if any additional countermeasures should be
  considered for implementation in the City

  31
 10.2.3 Implementation Strategies
The opportunities outlined in this report presents potential strategies and measures that can be
implemented at both a systemic level and specific locations within the city. However, the actual
implementation of these measures will depend on the availability of funding and resources, and
its important to note that this guidance is preliminary and subject to change. In the near-term
and mid-term, the City can focus its efforts on the following key areas of emphasis.

  •  Stopped- Controlled Intersection Improvements
  •  Vulnerable User Improvement
  •  Aggressive Driving Improvement

The analysis conducted at the citywide level has identified these factors as the most common
contributors to collisions within the City. The countermeasure opportunities discussed earlier in
this report, which encompass both systemic improvements and project-specific enhancements,
can serve as a foundation for developing projects in locations where addressing these focus
areas would yield the greatest benefits. These countermeasures were determined by examining
the causes and types of collisions and devising strategies to address the specific conditions
associated with them. By using citywide collision rates, projects aimed at addressing these
focus areas can be developed with a favorable benefit-to-cost ratio, even in locations with little
or no history of collisions but with conditions that could contribute to future incidents. For
location-specific improvements, the City can utilize benefit-cost ratio calculations to prioritize
projects as funding and resources become available.

This project prioritization process will help the City be ready for the funding opportunities
identified in Section 9. Project prioritization will also help to guide the projects as they are taking
into the design and construction project. Prioritization can be based on cost and ease of
installation. Coordination with City departments will be key in the completion of these
implementations.

The City can also plan to implement the non-engineering improvements identified throughout
this report, including actions related to Enforcement, Education, and Emergency Services.
These actions will require coordination with internal and external stakeholders, such as City
departments, law enforcement, local government organizations, and local community
organizations. Early buy-in and engagement from these stakeholders will be key to the success
of these actions.

To aid in these actions, the City can assemble a ‘Task Force’ of representatives from different
City departments, such as Public Works, Development Services, and Public Safety. This task
force will be instrumental in the monitoring, analysis update, project development and project
implementation outlined in this plan.

 10.3 Next Steps
The City has completed the LRSP to guide the process of future transportation safety
improvements for years to come. In addition to the actions identified in the Implementation Plan,
the City can perform the following to guide the success of this LRSP and the safety efforts
overall.

  •  Develop investment programs to help achieve the City’s crash reduction goals.
  •  Work with state and partner agencies on implementation of large-scale programs and
  policies;
  •  Incorporate safety analysis findings in future updates of safety programs;
  •  Monitor statewide safety priorities, guidance, and funding opportunities.

 Behavioral Safety Countermeasures
This appendix provides an overview of the implementation of behavioral safety countermeasures
in the Local Roadway Safety Plan. The primary objective is to address the critical issue of
promoting safe behaviors among road users, focusing on drivers, pedestrian, and cyclists. By
targeting specific behaviors such as speeding, distracted driving, failure to yield, and disobeying
traffic signals, the aim is to create a culture of responsible and cautious road use in the City of
Palmdale. This section outlines potential strategies including education campaigns, enforcements
efforts, and targeted interventions, with the ultimate goal of reducing fatal and severe injuries in
the local roadways.

Education Campaigns

To raise awareness about safe driving
practices and the potential consequences
of risky behaviors. These campaigns can
use various platforms such as social media,
community events, and informational
materials to educate road users on the
importance of following traffic rules and
being mindful of their actions on the roads.

Educational  campaigns  increase
awareness among road users about the
significance of following traffic rules and
regulations. By providing information on safe driving practices, the responsibilities of pedestrians,
and rights of cyclists, these campaigns ensure that individuals have a clear understanding of their
role in promoting road safety. These campaigns aim to bring about a change in behavior by
highlighting the risks associated with unsafe actions. By emphasizing the potential consequences
of behaviors like speeding, distracted driving, and failure to yield, these campaigns encourage
individuals to adopt safer practices and make responsible choices on the road. Additionally,
education campaigns focus on equipping road users with the necessary knowledge and skills to
navigate the road safely. By providing information on defensive driving techniques, pedestrian
safety guidelines, and cycling best practices, individuals are empowered to make informed
decisions and take appropriate actions to prevent collisions. Moreover, these campaigns foster
community engagement and participation in promoting local roadway safety. By involving local
residents, schools, businesses, and community organizations, a collective effort is made to create
a culture of safety behaviors. Through consistent reinforcement of safe practices and ongoing
education, these campaigns can instill a sense of responsibility and caution in road users, leading
to a significant reduction in fatal and serious injuries on local roadways over time.

Enforcement Efforts

Through collaboration with law enforcement agencies, stricter monitoring and enforcement of
traffic laws can discourage unsafe action. Targeted enforcement operations are conducted in

 areas with a history of collisions or high-risk behaviors, with the aim of deterring violations and

Enforcement ensures that individuals adhere to traffic rules and regulations. By enforcing
consequences for unsafe actions authorities create a deterrent effect and encourage compliance
with safe practices. This enforcement serves as a reinforcement mechanism, reinforcing the
importance of following traffic rules and holding individuals accountable for their actions on the
road.

Targeted Interventions

 To address specific areas of behaviors that pose a higher risk to road safety, countermeasures
incorporate targeted interventions. These interventions include installing traffic calming

collision locations. By implementing these

Targeted interventions are a more focused

to create a culture of responsible and cautious road use in our community. By addressing efforts
to address specific areas of behaviors, it can maximize the effectiveness of countermeasures

recognizing that humans make mistakes and aiming to establish a forgiving road system that
minimizes the impact of these errors. Through these efforts, it is anticipated a significant
reduction in accidents and injuries on local roadways, ultimately enhancing overall road safety.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council adopt Resolution No. CC 2024-087, a
Resolution of the City Council of the City of Palmdale authorizing the issuance of Special
Tax Bonds for the City of Palmdale Community Facilities District No. 2022-3 (Ritter
Ranch Phase 1 Public Facilities) and approving related documents and actions.

BACKGROUND

RdR Development Holdings, LLC is the property owner of the Phase 1 property portion
of the Community Facilities District No. 2022-3 (“CFD 2022-3”) and has requested that
the City proceed with the approval of the first series of Special Tax Bonds (“Bonds”) for
CFD 2022-3. Certain actions are required by the City Council for the issuance of the
Bonds.

DISCUSSION

The Phase 1 development contains 1,180 residential units. These units will be built over
time. RdR Development Holdings, LLC (Master Developer) wish to issue the first series
of Bonds now to be supported by the Special Taxes on all of the 688 detached single-
family units. This encompasses all the units in Phase 1A and 135 units in Phase 1B. A
future series of Bonds (subject to future City Council consideration and action) is
proposed for 2026, to be secured by the remaining 492 attached residential units.

The Special Taxes generated by the detached single-family units supports approximately
$33.4 million in Bonds. This will provide funding of an estimated $28.4 million in
infrastructure improvements. A reserve fund for the Bonds is also anticipated to be
funded with Bond proceeds. The following table provides the anticipated size of the bond
issue, including funding of the costs of issuance and capitalized interest. Capitalized
interest is used to pay debt service on the Bonds during the first two tax years until taxes
can be levied.

 Cost of Issuance  $  808,000
 Reserve Fund  1,226,000
 Capitalized Interest through 9/1/2026  2,830,000
 City Administrative Fees  86,000
 Construction Fund  28,405,000
 Par Amount of Bonds Issued  $33,355,000
  $16,465,000
All costs associated with the Bonds will be paid out of proceeds from the issuance of the
bonds as outlined below.

 Bond Counsel/Disclosure Counsel  $80,000
 Municipal Advisor  80,000
 Special Tax Consultant  19,000
 Trustee  10,000
 Staff Reimbursable Costs  35,000
 Total Fixed Costs  $224,000
 Underwriting  584,000
 Total Expected Issuance Expenses  $808,000

It is anticipated that the Bonds will be issued on February 27, 2025.

Special Tax Bonds typically mature in 30 years. These Bonds will mature in 2064, a forty-
year maturity. This longer maturity was negotiated with the RdR parties as part of the
creation of CFD 2022-3 and cancellation of the City’s CFD 93-1 (Ritter Ranch) Special
Tax Bonds currently secured by the Phase 1 property. The interest rate is expected to
be 6%.

The infrastructure expected to be funded with this current series of Bonds include street
improvements, domestic water facilities, and sewer and storm drain facilities. The City
and the Master Developer are parties to an Acquisition Agreement, dated as of
November 1, 2022, relating to the construction by the Master Developer of some of the
infrastructure for CFD 2022-3 and the parties are required to approve a Supplement No.
1 to Acquisition Agreement (Acquisition Agreement Supplement) to update the type of
facilities to be financed and the budget for the infrastructure to be constructed by the
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Adopt Resolution CC 2024-087
November 20, 2024
Page 3

Master Developer. The Acquisition Agreement Supplement will be presented for
consideration at a future meeting.

The Bonds will be sold by Hilltop Securities Inc. to the Master Developer or a related entity
such as Preston Hollow Community Capital (Bondholder). Due to the significant amount
of infrastructure required to be built to support the first phase of development, remaining
land use approvals and other issues affecting the ability to build homes in Phase 1, the
Bondholder will hold the Bonds as an investment until such time as certain transfer
restrictions are lifted. The Bonds should be held by sophisticated investors during the
buildout period in case development delays occur or other impediments to development
materialize. Currently there are no improvements in CFD 2022-3 and the assessed value
of the 235 acres is only $1,156,708. The value of the property is an important factor in
determining the investment quality of the Bonds.

The Master Developer has advised that, given the land use entitlements that have been
obtained for Phase 1A and a portion of Phase 1B and are in process for the remainder of
Phase 1B, and the expected use of proceeds of the Bonds to finance infrastructure
improvements incident to the development of the property in the CFD, the fair market
value of the property may be significantly greater than its current County-assessed value,
and the fair market value of the property will in any event increase as infrastructure
improvements are completed and homes are constructed in the CFD. However, prudent
provisions have been included in the Fiscal Agent Agreement that only allow the Bonds
to be transferred to other designated sophisticated investors, or used as security for
lenders to the Bondholder, until the appraised value to the lien of the Bonds is at least 3:1
and all land use entitlements and zoning for development of all 1,180 residential units is
obtained.

A preliminary limited offering memorandum, describing CFD 2022-3, the Bonds, the
Master Developer, the proposed development, and the Bond transfer restrictions was
prepared by staff and the Disclosure Counsel, with input from the City’s bond counsel and
from the Master Developer.

Approval of the financing requires that the City adopt a resolution authorizing distribution
of the preliminary limited offering memorandum in connection with the bond sale, sale of
the Bonds on certain terms and conditions, and execution of various documents in
connection with the bond sale by the City Manager and the Director of Operations.

The parameters for the Bond sale are: (1) the par amount of the Bonds cannot exceed
$46,000,000, (2) the true interest cost must be less than 7% and (3) the underwriters’
discount cannot exceed 1.75% of the par amount of the Bonds.

The City Council resolution also approves the form of the following documents:

   Section 4.03. Reserve Fund.

  (A)  Establishment of Reserve Fund. There is hereby established as a separate
  fund to be held by the Fiscal Agent, the Community Facilities District No. 2022-3 (Ritter
  Ranch Phase 1 Public Facilities) Reserve Fund, to the credit of which a deposit shall be
  made as required by Section 3.02(A), which deposit is equal to the Reserve Requirement
  as of the Closing Date, and deposits shall be made as provided in Section 2.14(C),
  subclause second of clause (ii) of the second paragraph of Section 3.04(A), and Section
  3.04(B). Moneys in the Reserve Fund shall be held by the Fiscal Agent for the benefit of
  the Owners of the Bonds as a reserve for the payment of principal of, and interest and any
  premium on, the Bonds and shall be subject to a lien in favor of the Owners of the Bonds.

  (B)  Use of Reserve Fund. Except as otherwise provided in this Section, all
  amounts deposited in the Reserve Fund shall be used and withdrawn by the Fiscal Agent
  solely for the purpose of making transfers to the Bond Fund in the event of any deficiency
  at any time in the Bond Fund of the amount then required for payment of the principal of,
  and interest and any premium on, the Bonds or, in accordance with the provisions of this
  Section, for the purpose of redeeming Bonds from the Bond Fund.

  (C)  Transfer of Excess of Reserve Requirement. Whenever, on the Business
  Day before any Interest Payment Date, or on any other date at the request of an Authorized
  Officer, the amount in the Reserve Fund exceeds the Reserve Requirement, the Fiscal
  Agent shall provide written notice to the City of the amount of the excess and shall transfer
  an amount equal to the excess from the Reserve Fund to the Bond Fund to be used for the
  payment of interest on the Bonds on the next Interest Payment Date in accordance with
  Section 4.02.

  (D)  Transfer for Rebate Purposes. Amounts in the Reserve Fund shall be
  withdrawn, at the written request of an Authorized Officer, for purposes of making
  payment to the federal government to comply with Section 6.02.

  (E)  Transfer When Balance Exceeds Outstanding Bonds. Whenever the
  balance in the Reserve Fund exceeds the amount required to redeem or pay the Outstanding
  Bonds, including interest accrued to the date of payment or redemption and premium, if
  any, due upon redemption, the Fiscal Agent shall transfer the amount in the Reserve Fund
  to the Bond Fund to be applied, on the next succeeding Interest Payment Date for which
  notice of redemption can timely be given to the payment and redemption, in accordance
  with Section 4.02 or 2.03, as applicable, of all of the Outstanding Bonds. In the event that
  the amount so transferred from the Reserve Fund to the Bond Fund exceeds the amount
  required to pay and redeem the Outstanding Bonds, the balance in the Reserve Fund shall
  be transferred to the City to be used for any lawful purpose under the Law.

  Notwithstanding the foregoing, no amounts shall be transferred from the Reserve
  Fund pursuant to this Section 4.03(E) until after (i) the calculation, pursuant to Section
  6.02, of any amounts due to the federal government following payment of the Bonds and
  withdrawal of any such amount under Section 4.03(D) for purposes of making such

  29

  Fiscal Agent.

  (F)  Transfer Upon Special Tax Prepayment. Whenever Special Taxes are
  prepaid and Bonds are to be redeemed with the proceeds of such prepayment pursuant to
  Section 2.03(A)(iii) and 4.02(B)(ii), an amount equal to the “Reserve Fund Credit,” as
  described in and computed pursuant to Section I of the Rate and Method of Apportionment
  (as such amount is confirmed by the Finance Director to the Fiscal Agent) shall be
  transferred on the Business Day prior to the redemption date by the Fiscal Agent to the
  Bond Fund to be applied to the redemption of the Bonds pursuant to Section 2.03(A)(iii).

  (G)  Investment. Moneys in the Reserve Fund shall be invested in accordance
  with Section 6.01. One Business Day before each Interest Payment Date, interest earnings
  and profits resulting from said investment shall be transferred by the Fiscal Agent to the
  Bond Fund to be used by the Fiscal Agent for the purposes of such fund, but any such
  transfer shall be made only to the extent that following such transfer the amount on deposit
  in the Reserve Fund equals the then Reserve Requirement.

   ARTICLE V

  OTHER COVENANTS OF THE CITY

  Section 5.01. Punctual Payment. The City will punctually pay or cause to be paid the
principal of and interest and any premium on, the Bonds when and as due in strict conformity with
the terms of this Agreement and any Supplemental Agreement, and it will faithfully observe and
perform all of the conditions, covenants and requirements of this Agreement and all Supplemental
Agreements and of the Bonds.Limited Obligation. The Bonds are limited obligations of the City
on behalf of the District and are payable solely from and secured solely by the Special Tax
Revenues and the amounts in the Bond Fund (including the Capitalized Interest Account and the
Special Tax Prepayments Account therein), the Reserve Fund and the Special Tax Fund created
hereunder.Extension of Time for Payment. In order to prevent any accumulation of claims for
interest after maturity, the City shall not, directly or indirectly, extend or consent to the extension
of the time for the payment of any claim for interest on any of the Bonds and shall not, directly or
indirectly, be a party to the approval of any such arrangement by purchasing or funding said claims
for interest or in any other manner. In case any such claim for interest shall be extended or funded,
whether or not with the consent of the City, such claim for interest so extended or funded shall not
be entitled, in case of default hereunder, to the benefits of this Agreement, except subject to the
prior payment in full of the principal of all of the Bonds then Outstanding and of all claims for
interest which shall not have been so extended or funded.Against Encumbrances. The City will
not encumber, pledge or place any charge or lien upon any of the Special Tax Revenues or other
amounts pledged to the Bonds superior to or on a parity with the pledge and lien herein created for
the benefit of the Bonds, except as permitted by this Agreement.Books and Records. The City
will keep, or cause to be kept, proper books of record and accounts, separate from all other records
and accounts of the City, in which complete and correct entries shall be made of all transactions
relating to the Special Tax Revenues. Such books of record and accounts shall at all times during
City business hours and following reasonable prior written notice be subject to the inspection of
the Owners of not less than ten percent (10%) of the principal amount of the Bonds then
Outstanding, or their representatives duly authorized in writing.Protection of Security and Rights
of Owners. The City will preserve and protect the security of the Bonds and the rights of the
Owners, and will warrant and defend their rights against all claims and demands of all persons.
From and after the delivery of any of the Bonds by the City, the Bonds shall be incontestable by
the City.Compliance with Law. The City will comply with all applicable provisions of the Law
in administering the District; provided that the City shall have no obligation to advance any of its
own funds for any purpose whatsoever under this Agreement.Continuing Disclosure. The City
hereby covenants and agrees that it will comply with and carry out all of the provisions of the
Continuing Disclosure Agreement. Notwithstanding any other provision of this Agreement, failure
of the City to comply with the Continuing Disclosure Agreement shall not be considered a default
on the Bonds or a breach of any other provision of this Agreement; however the Participating
Underwriter or any 2025 Bondholder may take such actions as may be necessary and appropriate
to compel performance by the City of its obligations under the Continuing Disclosure Agreement,
including seeking mandate or specific performance by court order.Federal Guarantee
Prohibition. The City shall not take any action or permit or suffer any action to be taken if the
result of the same would be to cause any of the 2025 Bonds to be “federally guaranteed” within
the meaning of section 149(b) of the Code.Collection of Special Tax Revenues. The City shall
comply with all requirements of the Law so as to assure the timely collection of Special Tax
  31
09960.00000\42886166.2
 Revenues, including without limitation, the enforcement of delinquent Special Taxes.On or about
July 1 of each year, the Fiscal Agent shall provide the Finance Director with a notice stating the
amounts then on deposit in the Bond Fund and the accounts therein and the Reserve Fund. The
receipt of such notice by the Finance Director shall in no way affect the obligations of the City
under the following three paragraphs. Upon receipt of such notice, the Finance Director shall
communicate with the Auditor or other appropriate official of the County to ascertain the relevant
parcels on which the Special Taxes are to be levied, taking into account any parcel splits during
the preceding and then current year. In computing the amount of Special Taxes to be levied, the
City shall take into account funds available in the Bond Fund and the accounts therein and the
Special Tax Fund to make the payment of debt service on the Bonds due on the Interest Payment
Dates occurring in the next calendar year, along with any transfers of investment earnings pursuant
to Sections 4.03(C) or 4.03(G) to the Bond Fund expected to occur on such Interest Payment Date.

  The City shall effect the levy of the Special Taxes from time to time during each Fiscal
Year in accordance with the Ordinance and the Rate and Method of Apportionment. Specifically,
the City shall compute the amount of Special Taxes to be so levied each Fiscal Year before the
final date on which the Auditor will accept the transmission of the Special Tax amounts for the
parcels within the District for inclusion on the next secured or unsecured, as applicable, real
property tax roll. Upon the completion of the computation of the amounts of the levy, the City
shall prepare or cause to be prepared, and shall transmit to the Auditor, such data as the Auditor
requires to include the levy of the Special Taxes on the next real property tax roll. The Special
Taxes so levied shall be payable and be collected in the same manner and at the same time and in
the same installment as the taxes on property levied on the tax roll are payable, and have the same
priority, become delinquent at the same times and in the same proportionate amounts and bear the
same proportionate penalties and interest after delinquency as do the general ad valorem taxes
levied on the County tax roll.

  In the event that the City determines to levy all or a portion of the Special Taxes by means
of direct billing of the property owners within the District, and to the extent permitted by the
Ordinance, the City shall, not less than forty-five (45) days prior to the first Interest Payment Date
for which the levy is being made, send bills to the property owners in the District for Special Taxes
necessary to meet the financial obligations of the District due on the Interest Payment Dates for
which the levy is being made, said bills to specify that the amounts so levied shall be due and
payable in two equal installments with each installment due not less than thirty (30) days prior to
the related Interest Payment Date and each installment shall be delinquent if not paid when due.

  In any event, the City shall fix and levy the amount of Special Taxes within the District
required for the timely payment of principal of and interest on any Outstanding Bonds becoming
due and payable, including any necessary replenishment of the Reserve Fund to the amount of the
then Reserve Requirement and an amount estimated to be sufficient to pay the Administrative
Expenses, and shall take into account any prepayments of Special Taxes theretofore received by
the City. The Special Taxes so levied shall not exceed the maximum amounts as provided in the
Rate and Method of Apportionment.

  The Finance Director is hereby authorized to employ consultants to assist in computing the
levy of the Special Taxes hereunder and any reconciliation of amounts levied to amounts received.
The fees and expenses of such consultants and the costs and expenses of the Finance Director

 (including a charge for City staff time) in conducting its duties hereunder shall be an
Administrative Expense hereunder.

  Section 5.11. Further Assurances. The City will adopt, make, execute and deliver any
and all such further resolutions, instruments and assurances as may be reasonably necessary or
proper to carry out the intention or to facilitate the performance of this Agreement, and for the
better assuring and confirming unto the Owners of the rights and benefits provided in this
Agreement.No Arbitrage. The City shall not take, or permit or suffer to be taken by the Fiscal
Agent or otherwise, any action with respect to the proceeds of the 2025 Bonds which, if such action
had been reasonably expected to have been taken, or had been deliberately and intentionally taken,
on the date of issuance of the 2025 Bonds would have caused the 2025 Bonds to be “arbitrage
bonds” within the meaning of section 148 of the Code.Maintenance of Tax-Exemption. The
City shall take all actions necessary to assure the exclusion of interest on the 2025 Bonds from the
gross income of the owners of the 2025 Bonds to the same extent as such interest is permitted to
be excluded from gross income under the Code as in effect on the date of issuance of the 2025
Bonds.Covenant to Foreclose. The City hereby covenants with and for the benefit of the Owners
of the Bonds that it will order, and cause to be commenced as hereinafter provided, and thereafter
diligently prosecute to judgment (unless such delinquency is theretofore brought current), an action
in the superior court to foreclose the lien of any Special Tax or installment thereof not paid when
due as provided in the following paragraph. The Finance Director shall notify legal counsel of any
such delinquency of which it is aware, and such legal counsel shall commence, or cause to be
commenced, such proceedings.On or about August 15 of each Fiscal Year, the Finance Director
shall compare the amount of Special Taxes theretofore levied in the District to the amount of
Special Tax Revenues theretofore received by the City; and:

  (A)  Individual Delinquencies. If the Finance Director determines that any
  single parcel subject to the Special Tax in the District is delinquent in the payment of
  Special Taxes in the greater of (i) the aggregate amount of $5,000 or more, or (ii) the
  payment of four or more installments of Special Taxes levied on such parcel, then the
  Finance Director shall send or cause to be sent a notice of delinquency (and a demand for
  immediate payment thereof) to the property owner within 45 days of such determination,
  and (if the delinquency remains uncured), foreclosure proceedings shall be commenced by
  the City against the delinquent parcel within 90 days of such determination and shall be
  diligently pursued by the City to completion.

  (B)  Aggregate Delinquencies. If the Finance Director determines that the total
  amount of delinquent Special Tax for the prior Fiscal Year for the entire District (including
  the total of delinquencies under subsection (A) above), exceeds 5% of the total Special Tax
  due and payable for the prior Fiscal Year, the Finance Director shall notify or cause to be
  notified property owners who are then delinquent in the payment of Special Taxes (and
  demand immediate payment of the delinquency) within 45 days of such determination, and
  the City shall commence foreclosure proceedings within 90 days of such determination

directed are Permitted Investments as required hereunder, and which by their terms mature prior

described in clause (h) of the definition thereof; provided, however, that any such investment shall
